title: Blue Jacket (Weyapiersenwah)
summary: Shawnee war chief Blue Jacket (c. 1743–1810) fought Kentucky militias from his Ohio towns, raiding into Kentucky and negotiating at Limestone in 1787.
bodyMarkdown:
[Blue Jacket](/people/#blue-jacket), whose Shawnee name was Weyapiersenwah, was one of the hardest foes Kentucky ever faced. He was born around 1743. His early life is thin in the records. He first shows up in writing in 1773, living in a town on the Scioto in what is now Ohio.

The next year he fought at the Battle of Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore's War, alongside [Cornstalk](/stories/cornstalk-hokoleskwa-point-pleasant-to-fort-randolph/). When the Revolution came, he sided with Britain. The Shawnee saw the Kentucky stations as a threat to their southern hunting ground, and Blue Jacket's warriors raided them.

In 1786 [Benjamin Logan](/people/#benjamin-logan) led Kentucky militia north and burned Shawnee towns, Blue Jacket's among them. That raid is told in the story of [Moluntha and Logan's raid](/stories/moluntha-and-logans-raid-1786/). In 1787 Blue Jacket came to Limestone, now Maysville, to talk peace and trade prisoners. The truce did not last, and by 1788 his men were raiding Kentucky again.

His greatest years came next. Blue Jacket and the Miami leader [Little Turtle](/people/#little-turtle) led the warriors of the Northwest Confederacy in the [Northwest Indian War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northwest_Indian_War). In 1790 they beat Josiah Harmar's army, Kentucky militia included, as told in [Little Turtle and Hardin's defeat](/stories/little-turtle-and-hardins-defeat-1790/). In 1791 they destroyed [Arthur St. Clair's](/people/#arthur-st-clair) army on the Wabash. More than six hundred soldiers died. It is still counted the U.S. Army's worst defeat by Native forces.

The tide turned in 1794. [Anthony Wayne's](/people/#anthony-wayne) army, with Kentucky mounted volunteers, beat the confederacy at the [Battle of Fallen Timbers](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Fallen_Timbers), where Blue Jacket led the warriors. A year later he signed the [Treaty of Greenville](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/), which gave up most of what is now Ohio and ended the raids on Kentucky.

Blue Jacket lived on near Detroit and died around 1810. A story spread in the 1800s that he was a white captive named Marmaduke Van Swearingen. DNA testing in 2006 found no link to the Van Swearingen family, and most historians now treat him as Shawnee by birth.

## Kentucky today

Maysville, where Blue Jacket came to parley in 1787, is the seat of Mason County. His story runs through Kentucky's frontier wars from Point Pleasant to Greenville.
